activities.caption: three voices in one room — pair each with its tradition
activities.name: upHearMatch

config.prompt: Match each element of the hearing to the tradition it speaks for:

pairs.right: the rational model — goals, data, alternatives, evaluation
communicative practice — planning as structured public argument
the just city — who benefits, and who is absent from the room?

config.why: A planner fluent in only one of the three vocabularies is fluent in only part of their own job.

activities.anchor: Three overlapping movements then built the profession
activities.caption: the founding movements — file each idea
activities.name: upMoveSort

buckets: monumental reform — City Beautiful & grand plans

items.label: beaux-arts civic centres — noble buildings, ennobled citizens
self-contained towns of about 30,000, ringed by permanent greenbelt
cholera traced to contaminated wells; sewers, piped water, paved streets

config.why: The sanitary insight — that urban form determines urban health — became the profession's charter, which is why planning still shares intellectual DNA with public health.

activities.caption: true or false — is zoning neutral?
activities.name: upZoneJudge

statements.s: Zoning is a neutral technical map of what belongs where.
statements.why: Minimum lot sizes and single-family-only districts — legal in the US for a century — function to exclude cheaper housing, and were often designed to.

statements.s: Redlining's effects persist in wealth and tree cover to this day.
statements.why: The 1930s federal maps graded minority neighbourhoods as unbankable.
Today's upzoning and missing-middle debates are the direct descendants of the exclusionary history — the just-city theorists' insistence.

activities.anchor: a forecast is advocacy with decimal points
activities.caption: when the machinery disciplines power — drag the divider
activities.name: upDataCompare

config.prompt: Better data, two outcomes — drag the divider:

before.label: goals genuinely shared
before.text: the machinery disciplines power — a comparable table over decades of costs and benefits, the discount rate argued openly, the choice documented

after.label: values in conflict
after.text: what to measure (traffic speed versus traveller time, property value versus housing cost) quietly decides who wins, decades before the hearing

config.why: Better data sharpens the analysis; it cannot choose the values, because choosing values is the politics.

activities.caption: audit the engagement — place it on Arnstein's ladder
activities.name: upArnPlace

config.prompt: A well-attended consultation whose agenda was fixed before anyone arrived: place it on Arnstein's ladder (1–7).
config.why: The participants were informed, consulted, and then ignored — the informing/consultation rungs — while wearing the vocabulary of the top. The ladder measures who decides, not who attends.

activities.caption: the just-city lineage — pair each theorist with their move
activities.name: upJustMatch

config.prompt: Match each theorist to what they added:

pairs.right: planning as distribution under capital — land, rent, and whose profit the plan serves
'the right to the city' — the just-city rallying cry
three tests from New York, London and Amsterdam: equity, diversity, democracy

config.why: Equity is distribution of benefit, diversity is who can live where, democracy is who decides — the normative question both predecessors skirted.

activities.caption: the triangle in motion — walk the trade-off
activities.name: upTriBranch

config.root: Fainstein's three tests trade off. Walk the triangle.

start.text: The well-organised homeowners' meeting votes down a modest apartment building. Democracy scored high. What about equity?

choices.label: Equity failed — the people who would live there were absent by definition
choices.feedback: A deeply democratic process can still produce exclusionary outcomes.

choices.label: Equity passed — the residents spoke and were heard
choices.feedback: Those residents spoke; the future residents could not — distribution is not the same as voice.

absent.text: The developer appeals, and the council approves the building over the neighbourhood's objections. What happened to democracy?

choices.label: It failed — an equitable outcome arrived top-down
choices.feedback: The triangle's other corner: an equitable outcome can arrive over the residents' objections.

choices.label: It passed — the council is elected
choices.feedback: Representative democracy is still democracy — but the record must own whose voices bound the decision.

present.text: The triangle never closes — which is why no single test can certify a plan as good on its own.

end.text: Neither corner wins cleanly: no single test — not the study, not the consultation, not the equity metric — certifies the plan. Document whom the decision binds.

config.why: Planning theory after 2000 is largely the management of that triangle.

config.prompt: Informal settlements — how many people do they house worldwide, roughly?
config.why: Roughly a billion — most of the world's urban growth happens outside formal planning, and the theory made for surveyed, zoned cities increasingly learns from the practice.
config.context: The implementation gap and informality are where adopted plans die in the budget process — policy actually happens in street-level discretion.
